original_question: Find an upper or asymptotic bound for C(n), the number of Costas arrays of order n, that matches the empirically observed decay of C(n)/n! more closely than the currently known O((n-1)!) bound. Also prove or disprove whether the ratio C(n)/n! decreases monotonically to 0.
target_in_paper: Section 4.2, Problem 4, “Bound on the number of Costas arrays.” ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right open problem: it asks for a sharper upper bound on C(n), the number of Costas arrays of order n, than the published C(n)=O((n−1)!) bound, and it also asks whether the density C(n)/n! decreases monotonically to 0. That is essentially the content of Problem 4. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, the question should define a Costas array (equivalently, Costas permutation): a bijection f:[n]→[n], where [n]={1,…,n}, such that all distance vectors (i−j, f(i)−f(j)) with 1≤j<i≤n are distinct; the paper also notes that addition here is ordinary addition in Z, not modular addition. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
It should state explicitly that n ranges over the positive integers and that C(n) counts Costas arrays of order n. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

The current published benchmark should be given in the paper’s exact form C(n)/n!=O(1/n), equivalently C(n)=O((n−1)!), because Problem 4 is posed against that specific upper bound. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

The empirical target is more specific than just ‘observed decay’: the paper says that for the known values up to n≤29, the ratio C(n)/n! seems to decay monotonically and at an exponential rate. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

The monotonicity clause should be formalized as a statement about the whole sequence {C(n)/n!}n≥1 unless one intentionally weakens it: prove or disprove that it is monotone decreasing and tends to 0. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

The paper asks for a bound that reflects the observed decay more closely; it does not require a particular proof strategy. The nearby ‘degrees of freedom’ discussion is contextual motivation, not part of the official statement of Problem 4. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency hypotheses are relevant here; the hidden assumptions to make explicit are purely combinatorial. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
refined_question: Let [n]={1,…,n}. For each n∈N*, let C(n) denote the number of Costas arrays of order n, equivalently the number of bijections f:[n]→[n] with the Costas property that the vectors {(i−j, f(i)−f(j)) : 1≤j<i≤n} are all distinct. Determine an upper bound for C(n) that improves on the published estimate C(n)=O((n−1)!) (equivalently, C(n)/n!=O(1/n)) and that reflects more closely the decay of the density C(n)/n! seen in the known data, which the paper reports as apparently monotone and exponential for n≤29. In particular, prove or disprove that the sequence {C(n)/n!}n≥1 is monotone decreasing and converges to 0. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
justification: The draft is a near-paraphrase of Problem 4 in §4.2, not of the neighboring problems. Section 4.2 first recalls the best published upper bound C(n)/n!=O(1/n)⇔C(n)=O((n−1)!), then states that the known data suggest monotone exponential decay of C(n)/n!, and then poses exactly the problem of finding a bound that better reflects that decay and deciding monotone convergence to 0. To make the question paper-faithful and self-contained, one must import the definition of Costas array from Definition 1 and the notation C(n) from Problem 1. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
